name: Kingdom of France (Louis XIV)

areaKm2.note: world_1700 France polygon = 481,560 km2 on the sphere. Lorraine was not French (1766).

population.note: HYDE via OWID: France (modern borders) 21,992,348 (1700). Lynn (Giant of the Grand Siecle ch. 1) works with ~20-21.5M for the kingdom c. 1700 after the famine of 1693-94 (1.3M deaths, Nine Years War article). Mid 21.5M.

urbanization.note: OWID urban share: France 7.0% (1700, de Vries-type, towns 10,000+); Bairoch 5,000+ runs higher, ~10-12%.

activePersonnel.note: Lynn, Giant of the Grand Siecle (1997) ch. 2, army size tables: after the Peace of Ryswick (1697) the army was cut to a peacetime establishment of ~140,000-150,000 (paper) in 1698-1700, rearming from late 1700 for the Spanish Succession; wartime peaks 362,000 in the Nine Years War (Lynn 2020 via the Nine Years War article) and 255,000-400,000 in 1701-14 (War of the Spanish Succession article). Plus ~20,000 navy personnel kept in service. Mid 165,000.

trainedReserves.note: Milice provinciale created 1688: ~25,000-30,000 per levy in the Nine Years War (Lynn ch. 11), disbanded 1697 and re-raised 1701; inscrits maritimes (sailors on the class rolls) excluded.

supportPersonnel.note: Navy personnel kept in commission in peacetime (~15,000-25,000, Colbert class system), Royal-Artillerie and bombardiers (~3,000-4,000), engineers (~300 ingenieurs du roi), administration (commissaires, intendants des armees).

mobilizationRatio.note: Peak paper strengths of 340,000-400,000 (Military Revolution article after Parker and Lynn) on ~21M = 1.6-1.9%; with navy and militia ~2.5%. Ceiling under the Ancien Regime ~3-5%.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: French and foreign (Swiss, German, Irish) infantry regiments incl. Gardes francaises and Gardes suisses at peacetime establishment (Lynn ch. 2 and 3). Reconstruction of the infantry share (~70% of the army); grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) to 0.75 (among the era best). Evidence: flintlock fusil adopted 1699 replacing matchlock and pike (socket bayonet), Vauban-designed equipment

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: long-service professionals, Martinet-style drill, veterans of 1688-97

count.note: Cavalerie regiments, gendarmerie and the Maison du Roi horse (Gardes du Corps, Mousquetaires) (Lynn ch. 3).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Maison du Roi the elite cavalry of Europe

count.note: Dragoon regiments (counted as light cavalry as in the France 1805 snapshot) and a few hussar companies.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: mounted infantry dragoons

count.note: Educated guess: field pieces in the arsenals and trains in peacetime; armies of the 1690s took 50-100 guns each into the field.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Valliere system only in 1732; artillery still civilian-contracted in part

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: Royal-Artillerie regiment from 1671 and bombardiers

count.note: Ships of the line: French naval peak strength 119 ships of the line in the Nine Years War (Van Nimwegen 2020 p. 67 via the Nine Years War article); after the 1690s losses (Barfleur-La Hougue) and laying up ~100 remained c. 1700 (Glete, Navies and Nations, isbn:91-22-01565-5).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: large, well-designed three-deckers and 70-80 gun ships

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: crews dispersed in peacetime; guerre de course replaced fleet action after 1694

count.note: Educated guess: frigates, light frigates and the Mediterranean galley corps (~40 galleys at Marseille, counted here).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: good privateering frigates (Jean Bart)

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: privateer crews skilled

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.75 (trained staff system, proven commanders). Evidence: War ministry of Louvois/Barbezieux, intendants, Vauban; Luxembourg (died 1695) and Catinat; Villars and Vendome still to prove themselves

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75. Evidence: standing regiments with corporate identity; venal officer corps

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Nine Years War ended in an exhausting draw, famine of 1693-94

weapons.note: Anchor: 5.5 between 1600 (5) and 1805 (6). Evidence: flintlock fusil and socket bayonet adopted 1699; pike abolished 1703

armor.note: Anchor: 5.3. Evidence: cuirasses for heavy cavalry only

ships.note: Anchor: 5.6. Evidence: three-deckers of the Colbert navy

fortification.note: Anchor: 5.8 near 6 (Vauban-type forts). Evidence: the Vauban pre carre of ~150 fortresses: the anchor's namesake

logistics.note: Anchor: 5.4. Evidence: Louvois magazine system and etapes (Lynn ch. 4, van Creveld ch. 1)

communications.note: Anchor: 5.2. Evidence: royal post, courier network

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years as the anchor table (1600 -> 5, 1805 -> 6). Evidence: cavalry screens, spies and merchant reports only; no aerial or signal intelligence

air.note: No aircraft or military balloons before 1783/1794.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Lynn ch. 1: war consumed ~75% of royal spending; royal revenue ~120-150M livres against national income ~1.5-2.0bn livres. Peacetime 1698-1700 ~3-4%; wartime 1690s ~8%.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: Colbertian manufactures, textiles, arms works (Saint-Etienne, Charleville); ~2/3 of output agricultural.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: grain self-sufficient in normal years but vulnerable (famines 1693-94, 1709).

annualCohort.note: population x 0.009-0.011 (mid 0.0095): in a pre-transition age structure (Wrigley and Schofield type, life expectancy ~30-35) males reaching 18 each year are about 0.9-1.1% of total population. Males only.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: royal roads (grands chemins) radiating from Paris before the Ponts et Chaussees corps (1716).

majorPorts.note: Brest, Toulon, Rochefort, Dunkirk, Le Havre, Saint-Malo, Marseille, Bordeaux, Nantes, Lorient.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: French merchant shipping c. 1700 (Colbert-era surveys suggest ~100,000-200,000 tons burden).

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld, Supplying War (isbn:0-521-54657-5) ch. 1: 17th-18th c. armies tied to magazines and bread ovens, operating ~5 marches (~100-150 km) beyond the nearest magazine or navigable river; requisition extends it in rich country.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~2M horses plus oxen and mules.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: familiar terrain, Vauban fortress belt (pre carre), loyal population; no harsh-climate depth.

notes: Snapshot = 1700, between Ryswick (1697) and the War of the Spanish Succession (Charles II of Spain died 1 Nov 1700). Population: kingdom of France in its 1700 borders; colonies are bases only. Personnel convention: regiments of the peacetime establishment and naval personnel in service are active; provincial militia (disbanded 1697, re-raised 1701) is trainedReserves. Lynn's paper strengths (printed book, not fetched) anchor the army; the Nine Years War and War of the Spanish Succession articles give the wartime peaks used as the upper bound context.
